solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: My behaviour’s pretentious in August

blocks.note: someone describing their own behaviour begins 'I'm'
behaving pretentiously is posing, putting on airs

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to showing off during the summer holiday month.
explanation.walkthrough: August looks like the month, but here it is the adjective (stress on the second syllable). A pretentious person might say I'M POSING, which runs together as IMPOSING.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, august means grand and majestic, inspiring awe, which is a close synonym of imposing.

clue.text: Like following trendy disc – Kind of Blue?

indicators.note: to follow is to come straight after, so one piece is placed behind another

blocks.note: what is trendy is in
slang: to dig something is to like it
a disc is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A jazz fan asks whether to follow fashion by playing the trendy record, Miles Davis's Kind of Blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Kind of Blue is the famous Miles Davis album, and DIG is jazz slang, which keeps the surface in the jazz club; the question mark warns the title is being read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigo is a deep violet-tinged shade, one particular variety within the range of blue colours.

clue.text: Plug old sinks in quiet space

indicators.note: in a down entry, a letter that sinks drops lower in the column, moving later in the word

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
room is space, as in 'room to move'
O is the abbreviation for old; it names which letter moves rather than adding a new one

explanation.surface: An old drain gets blocked somewhere in a quiet place.
explanation.walkthrough: The O standing for old is one of the two O's already in P+ROOM; in this down entry it sinks one place, below the M.
explanation.definitionFit: A plug is a piece of publicity for a product, and a promo is a short promotional advertisement doing the same job.

clue.text: Broadcaster declines to cover current news, or reveals all?

indicators.note: covering something means going round it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: Sky is a British satellite broadcaster
I is the symbol for electric current
news read as two lots of 'new', each N
a price that declines dips

explanation.surface: A TV channel, losing ratings, skips covering the latest news, or else bares everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is a British satellite TV company. 'News' is read as two lots of new; 'the skinny' is also slang for inside news, a bonus echo. The question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who goes swimming naked bares their whole body, so jokingly they show everything.

clue.text: How graduate starts merriment, putting away litres

indicators.note: putting something away removes it from view, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: glee is merriment
L is the abbreviation for litres

explanation.surface: A new graduate launches into partying and stops drinking by the litre.
explanation.walkthrough: Take L out of GLEE. 'Graduate starts' merely confirms that G, the graduate's initial, begins the word. 'How!' here is an exclamation of surprise, as in 'and how!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal interjections of surprise or emphasis, used as an amazed exclamation.

clue.text: Shadowy characters needing return fare from Asia

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so letters run backwards

blocks.note: shadowy means dim
mus, the plural of mu, are Greek characters

explanation.surface: Shady figures who need a ticket home from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return fare' reads as a travel ticket, but 'return' reverses the Greek letters and 'fare' means food.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim sum are small Chinese dumplings and snacks, a style of food originating in Asia.

clue.text: Lie falsely and kiss Holly?

indicators.note: something done falsely is not done straight, so the letters are set out wrongly

blocks.note: taken as written
X is a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Someone lies and then kisses a woman called Holly.
explanation.walkthrough: Holly looks like a name, but it is the plant; the question mark admits the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Ilex is the botanical genus name for the holly plants, so it is the scientific term for them.

clue.text: Focus on leading revolutionary beset by snub

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the word is flipped end to end
to be beset is to be surrounded on all sides, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a snub is a slight
the leading one is the top one

explanation.surface: Attention turns to a revolutionary leader who is being snubbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading revolutionary' reads as a rebel chief, but 'leading' gives TOP and 'revolutionary' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To spotlight something is to draw attention to it, a figurative use of shining a stage lamp.

clue.text: Crazy lines succeeded – two articles in part of paper

indicators.note: to line something is to cover its inside, so one piece forms a layer around another

blocks.note: crazy means mad
the indefinite article
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies
the definite article

explanation.surface: Mad writing got two pieces into a section of the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' looks like lines of text, but it is the verb, as in lining a coat: the crazy word wraps round everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: The masthead is the title block at the top of a newspaper's front page, one of its fixed sections.

clue.text: Skimpy garment‘s attractive with copper edging

indicators.note: an edging runs round the border, so one piece frames the other

blocks.note: copper is slang for a police officer, here a DI (Detective Inspector)
attractive means hot

explanation.surface: A revealing outfit looks sexy trimmed with copper-coloured braid.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper looks like the metal of a trim, but it is British slang for a police officer, here a Detective Inspector.
explanation.definitionFit: A dhoti is the loincloth worn by men in India, a single cloth wrapped round the waist that covers little.

clue.text: Loose cryptic clues cracked by revered figure

indicators.note: something cryptic is obscure and scrambled, so the letters are rearranged
something cracked is broken open, letting another piece in

blocks.note: taken as written
a hero is a revered figure

explanation.surface: Vague crossword clues finally solved by a respected expert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' suggests solving, which suits crossword clues, but here it means broken open to take HERO inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose in the old moral sense means promiscuous or immoral, and lecherous describes lustful, debauched behaviour.

clue.text: Pitch into African opponent of nanny state

indicators.note: one thing put into another ends up inside it

blocks.note: pitch is a tar-like substance
a Liberian comes from Liberia in West Africa

explanation.surface: Someone throws an African into a fight against an interfering government.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitch looks like a verb for throwing; it is the black tar.
explanation.definitionFit: A libertarian wants minimal government interference in private life, so opposes any intrusive, protective nanny state.

clue.text: Barefaced crook, at first, is inclined to get port

indicators.note: at first points to the very beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: opening letter of crook
to be inclined is to lean
is shortened to 's
a haven is a harbour or port

explanation.surface: A brazen crook is minded to seize a harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: Barefaced suggests shameless, which fits the crook; read literally, it means a face without a beard. The 's from 'is' slots in after LEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a bare face has no beard or stubble, which is exactly what a freshly shaved man shows.

clue.text: Land carp? It’s food for Americans

blocks.note: land is ground
to carp is to complain, or beef

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether landing a carp counts as American cuisine.
explanation.walkthrough: Land and carp both pretend to be about fishing, but they are the noun ground and the verb carp, to grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground beef is the American term for what the British call mince, minced cattle meat.

clue.text: Contemptuous remark about Liberal’s waffle

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: bah is a scornful exclamation
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A sneering comment on a Liberal politician's evasive talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Waffle could be the breakfast item; it is empty talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Waffle is long-winded empty talk, and blah is the dismissive word for meaningless verbiage.

clue.text: Car racing gives a new image to troublemakers

blocks.note: F1 is Formula One motor racing, with the 1 read as the letter I
to rebrand is to give a new image

explanation.surface: Motor racing gives a fresh image to its bad boys.
explanation.walkthrough: The digit 1 in F1 stands in for the letter I, a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A firebrand is a person who stirs up unrest and agitation, so firebrands are agitators causing trouble.

clue.text: Wife drops iron, making a mess of sweeping

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so those letters leave the word

blocks.note: taken as written
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
deranging means throwing into disorder

explanation.surface: A wife puts down the iron and makes a hash of the sweeping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweeping' looks like housework, but it is an adjective, as in sweeping changes. The wife's 'drops' is not setting the iron down but losing its chemical symbol from her own name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeping as an adjective means broad and extensive in scope, covering a large area of subjects.

clue.text: Collection of Kitty‘s whiskey and cool drinks

blocks.note: Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet
hip means cool, fashionable
a round is a set of drinks bought for a group

explanation.surface: A woman named Kitty owns a collection of whiskey and chilled drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitty looks like a name, but it is a shared pool of money. A whip-round is a British term for a quick collection among colleagues, say for a leaving present.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitty is a pooled fund, and a whip-round is the informal gathering of money that fills one.

clue.text: How thick dough’s regularly cut

indicators.note: cutting at regular intervals removes every other letter, keeping the rest

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A baker explains how thickly the dough is usually sliced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How thick' reads as a question about measurement, but it is an exclamation: how stupid!
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection is used to mock an obvious remark, meaning roughly 'how stupid can you be'.

clue.text: PC’s key bit of information applied, made bug-free

blocks.note: Del (Delete) is a key on a PC keyboard
a binary bit is 0 or 1; 0 is read as the letter O
applied means put to use

explanation.surface: A computer key bit of data is used to debug the software.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug-free' suggests software debugging; the answer means rid of lice. 'PC's key' gives DEL, the Delete key.
explanation.definitionFit: To delouse is to rid a person or animal of lice, so the past tense means made free of those insects.

clue.text: Kind of television screens one covered

indicators.note: to screen something is to shield it from view, holding it behind or inside

blocks.note: HD is high-definition television
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A sort of television shows one programme covered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screens' sounds like broadcasting, which suits television, but it means hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Hid is the past tense of hide, which means covered up or concealed from view.

clue.text: Charge nuisance, chronic cheat taking people in

indicators.note: chronic is slang for terrible, so the letters are badly mangled
taking something in means holding it inside

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous nuisance
taken as written
men are people

explanation.surface: An irritating habitual swindler is charged after conning people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chronic cheat' reads as a habitual swindler, but chronic is British slang for awful, signalling an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An impeachment is a formal accusation of wrongdoing against a public official, so a charge.

clue.text: Irish singer put up stage, loudly hosting party

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up makes it read bottom to top
a host holds guests inside, so one piece contains another

blocks.note: a leg is a stage of a journey
a do is a party
f (forte) is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: An Irish performer builds a stage and throws a noisy party on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the stage is turned upward; the loud letter then goes round the party. Bob Geldof fronted the Boomtown Rats and organised Live Aid.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Geldof is a famous Irish rock singer, frontman of the Boomtown Rats.

clue.text: Gruff ambassador ignored rows

indicators.note: what is ignored is left out of account, so letters are dropped

blocks.note: a gruff voice is hoarse
HE is His Excellency, the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: A grumpy envoy paid no attention to the arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: Rows suggests quarrels, which fits a gruff ambassador; it is the verb for rowing a boat. H and E come from opposite ends of HOARSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To oar a boat is to propel it with paddles, so oars works as a verb meaning rows.

clue.text: Pirate with a case for rare cups etc

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the outside letters are used

blocks.note: Long John Silver is the pirate in Treasure Island
W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written
outside letters of rare

explanation.surface: A pirate carries a box for valuable cups and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like a box for the treasure, but it signals the outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Silverware covers cups, trophies, cutlery and plates made of silver, so etc stands for the rest.

clue.text: Fighter in a ring, someone close to you

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside another

blocks.note: a MiG is a Russian fighter jet
taken as written
a ring is shaped like an O

explanation.surface: A boxer in the ring is someone very near to you.
explanation.walkthrough: Fighter and ring suggest boxing, but the fighter is a jet and the ring is a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend, used informally in English for a close companion or pal.

clue.text: Survey opinion

blocks.note: first meaning: to look over or inspect
second meaning: a personal belief or judgement

explanation.walkthrough: Survey and opinion together suggest an opinion poll, but they are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to look over a scene, and as a noun it means a point of view or belief.

clue.text: Wine you picked up in southern French city

indicators.note: picked up as on a radio, meaning heard, so a sound is spelt out
in puts one piece inside another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
Avignon is a city in southern France
the letter U is pronounced like you

explanation.surface: Someone collected you in a southern French city, where the wine flows.
explanation.walkthrough: U goes inside AVIGNON after its first letter, with S in front. Avignon is fittingly in wine country.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauvignon is a grape variety and the wine made from it, such as Sauvignon Blanc.

clue.text: Actor brags, bagging Golden Globe?

indicators.note: to bag something is to hold it inside, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: actOR Brags

explanation.surface: An actor boasts after winning a Golden Globe award.
explanation.walkthrough: The Golden Globes are film awards, which suits the actor; the question mark signals a literal golden globe.
explanation.definitionFit: An orb is a sphere, and the royal regalia include a golden one topped by a cross.

clue.text: Goddess, an incarnation of Diana?

indicators.note: an incarnation is a new embodiment, so the same letters take another form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asks whether a goddess is a reincarnation of the huntress Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: Diana is herself a goddess, which makes her look like the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a naiad is a water nymph, a minor female deity of rivers and springs.

clue.text: Cook miserable wraps in pan

blocks.note: to do food is to cook it, as in 'done to a turn'
feeling miserable is feeling down

explanation.surface: A grumpy cook wraps food up in a frying pan.
explanation.walkthrough: Pan looks like a cooking pot, but it is the verb meaning to criticise harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan a play is to slate it, and to do someone down is to belittle or disparage them.

clue.text: Batter’s opening run before wrong dismissal

indicators.note: an opening is a start, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: first letter of batter
to run is to rush
something off is wrong, as in off milk

explanation.surface: A cricket opening batsman scores a run before being wrongly given out.
explanation.walkthrough: Batter, opening, run and dismissal all suggest cricket, a British bat-and-ball game, but only the B of batter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A brush-off is a curt rejection, an abrupt refusal to pay attention to someone.
